title: The Lunchbox Mystery (Hook)
text: Have you ever found a tiffin box in your bag on Monday morning that you forgot to wash on Friday? What did the food inside look like? And what was that strange, sour smell?

title: What Happened? (Socratic Thinking)
text: Why do you think the food changed its color and started smelling bad? If you eat it, will you get energy or will you get sick? What invisible things might be growing on it?

content.title: Fungus Growing on Bread (Discovery)
content.description: Watch how tiny spores land on the moist bread and start growing into thread-like structures.

title: Food Spoilage (The Reveal)
text: When food gets a bad smell, changes color, or has cotton-like threads growing on it, we say the food has **spoiled**. This happens because of tiny organisms like bacteria and fungi (mould) that grow on moist food.

content.definition: The process by which food becomes bad and unfit for eating.

content.question: Which of these is NOT a sign that food has spoiled?
options: It has green or black patches.

title: Think and Tell (Reflection)
text: Imagine you are explaining to your younger sibling why they shouldn't eat an apple that has a soft, brown, smelly patch on it. What words would you use?

title: Microbes Everywhere! (Connection)
text: This connects to what we learn about diseases. The same kinds of tiny living things (microorganisms) that spoil our food can sometimes cause stomach aches if they go inside our bodies!

content.title: Be a Food Detective (Mastery)
content.text: Go to your kitchen and look at 3 packed food items (like biscuits or bread). Find the 'Expiry Date' or 'Use By' date on the packet. This date tells us when the food might start spoiling!

content.title: Wastage vs. Spoilage
content.text: Students often confuse 'Spoilage' and 'Wastage'. Spoilage is when food naturally goes bad. Wastage is when we take too much food on our plate and throw good food in the dustbin.

title: The Mango Mystery (Hook)
text: Mangoes only grow during the hot summer months. But wait... you eat mango pickles (achaar) and Aam Papad (Mamidi Tandra) even in winter! How is that possible?

title: Stopping the Spoilage (Socratic Thinking)
text: If a fresh mango spoils in a few days, what are we doing differently to make the pickle last for an entire year without spoiling in a jar? What do we add to it?

content.title: Drying in the Sun (Discovery)
content.description: See how the heat from the sun removes water from the mango pulp. Microorganisms need water to grow!

title: Food Preservation (The Reveal)
text: To stop food from spoiling, we use **Food Preservation**. We remove moisture by drying it in the sun, or we add lots of salt, oil, or sugar. Bacteria and fungi cannot grow easily without water or in too much salt/sugar!

content.definition: Methods used to keep food safe from spoiling for a long time.

content.title: Etymology Hint
content.text: The word 'Preserve' comes from Latin: 'pre' (beforehand) + 'servare' (to keep safe). So we are keeping the food safe beforehand, so it doesn't spoil later!

content.question: Which of these things is added to a raw mango to make a pickle that lasts a year?

title: Why 4 Weeks? (Reflection)
text: Making Mamidi Tandra (Aam Papad) takes 4 weeks of continuous drying in the sun. Why do you think it is so important to remove every single drop of water from it?

title: Science of Evaporation (Connection)
text: This connects to the concept of 'Evaporation' from science! The heat of the sun turns the liquid water in the mango pulp into gas, leaving behind only the solid, sweet mango layer.

content.title: Your Preservation Project (Mastery)
content.text: Ask your grandparents or parents about one food item they preserve at home (like making potato chips, pickles, or drying mint leaves). Write down the steps they follow!
